title: Lecture 13. Psychological testing
summary:
1 Types of diagnostic methods used in prevention

2 Psychological screening testing

3 Problems in developing psychological tests

1 Types of diagnostic methods used in prevention

There are various classifications for grouping the vast number of methods called psychological tests. When discussed in the context of prevention tasks, all of them can be conveniently divided into three types of methods (this division is conditional, and some methods cannot always be unambiguously assigned to one type).

1. Clinical scales. These methods essentially reproduce the diagnostic logic of a physician and use clinical criteria for a specific disease to make a diagnosis. Initially, these scales were used by doctors themselves, reading questions to patients, but now such tests can be easily found and taken online. The most famous such tests are, for example, the anxiety and depression scales developed by American psychiatrist Aaron Beck.

As a rule, these are short methods used only to confirm a diagnosis. Their main difference is that they only ask questions about the problem (i.e., about the resulting variable). In this case – about symptoms.

2. Screening scales (from English "screening" – selection, sifting) – methods that are usually called psychological tests. They are relatively short and are used in prevention for rapid initial identification of at-risk individuals from a large group. Their peculiarity is that, as a rule, they assess only factorial, but not resulting variables, meaning questions are asked about the factors and manifestations of the problem, but not about the problem itself. It is assumed that this fundamentally increases the reliability of the results obtained.

3. Comprehensive assessment methods (from English "assessment") – a comprehensive evaluation of an individual and their real or potential risk factors – family, social situation, past experience, mental and physical health, etc. Such methods are addressed to individuals from risk groups for their long-term individual preventive support. The next lecture will be dedicated to these methods.

Overall, the logic of prevention has a funnel-like structure, which with each step focuses on increasingly pronounced risk groups. In this logic, survey methods can be arranged in the following sequence:

Epidemiological studies or population (sociological) surveys – used to characterize social risk groups (without personal assessments) Psychological screening tests – used to identify groups with personal risk assessments within certain social groups. Comprehensive assessment methods are used for a thorough evaluation of specific individuals and their subsequent long-term preventive support. Clinical scales – used for diagnosing or confirming a diagnosis for specific individuals. 2. Psychological Screening Testing Such methods are typically a short research procedure used for the initial identification of individuals at high risk of behavioral disorders. Such screening usually does not allow for diagnostic conclusions but is intended for studying large groups of students and selecting individual children from them who require a more detailed assessment, specialist attention, or full professional help.

Psychological screening tests are completed by the children themselves. Completion time can range from 5 to 30 minutes, depending on the amount of information required from the adolescent. In any case, screening is conducted using a standardized method designed to collect specific information. The subject of such methods can include behavioral characteristics such as: level of anxiety and experienced stress, level of neuropsychic tension, sociometric status, self-esteem level, relationships, etc.

It is important to emphasize that such methods allow not only to determine the fact of problematic behavior that has occurred but also to predict the risk of problematic behavior forming before it actually happens, for example, the first drug use! Examples of such methods include: "Adolescent Chemical Dependency Inventory (ACDI)", "Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT-C)", "Crime Cycle Package (CCP)", "Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST)", and many others.

A strong point of screening testing is the possibility of full coverage of students in an educational organization and the ability to compare and generalize test results with other organizations where it is conducted (using the same method). Disadvantages of this method include significant time and organizational costs for conducting the testing and subsequent processing of results. Also, a drawback of this method is the generally low reliability of psychological tests.

The most important feature of this diagnostic tool is that it targets factorial, but not resulting variables!, meaning questions are asked about the factors and manifestations of the problem, but not about the problem itself (see diagram below):

. On the one hand, this fundamentally increases the reliability of the results obtained, as the respondent does not understand the exact purpose of the study they are participating in. This means they do not resist the true goal of the study and provide reliable answers (which they can easily distort when responding to clinical scales where the subject of the study is obvious). However, this increase in response reliability comes, on the other hand, with growing methodological complexities in developing such methods.

3. Problems in Developing Psychological Tests The procedure for creating a diagnostic method includes the following stages.

1 Development of a Theoretical Model

The purpose of the model is to describe the problem being solved as closely to real life as possible. For example, we want to create a method for assessing the risk and predicting drug use in adolescents. To develop factorial variables (leading to the resulting variable, which is the onset and development of drug use), the first step is to create a list of all possible statements about the causes of drug use in adolescents.

Sources of such statements may include, for example:

models already described in the literature on this problem, research results, preferably from current surveys of representatives of the target risk group, expert judgments, where specialists dealing with adolescent deviance describe the adolescents they encounter. In doing so, they describe the problems, typical manifestations of these problems, situations in which these problems arise, and measures to overcome them. These procedures help overcome the subjectivity of method developers, their intuition, and their own implicit theories stemming from their personal experience.

2 Scaling of Statements

The obtained statements are divided into several groups, describing different aspects of adolescent behavior. Each group of statements characterizes one of the factors of the studied problem. The more statements are true for an adolescent, the higher their level of drug use risk. This implies both the number of statements and their degree of expression, if the answers to the statements – questions of the future method – are also scaled.

3 Validation

Carried out during pilot studies. For the purpose of selecting significant statements, the following are conducted:

a) Expert evaluations – specialists whose activities are related to adolescent behavior assess the entire list of initial statements in terms of their significance for evaluating the problem (in our case, the risk of drug use), for example, on a five-point scale. After this, the least significant statements are filtered out.

b) Pilot survey of representatives of risk groups. The risk assessment method must be validated on representatives of the risk group on which it will be used in the future. This speaks to the importance of the approach to forming the sample on which the method will be tested. Participants in such a study answer a pilot version of the questionnaire; they may also be asked to evaluate how clear the question formulations are. The purpose of the study is to filter out poorly performing statements, which is determined by various statistical criteria.

Ultimately, only those statements that are relevant to the problem under study are selected for use in the method. The evaluation results obtained from various sources are taken into account.

Validity is the extent to which test results correspond to the characteristic it is intended to measure. Despite the variety of types of validity found in the literature, they can be reduced to three types.

a) Content validity: to what extent do the test results measure exactly what needs to be measured? The simplest example here is testing at the end of a training course. The test structure must correspond to the course structure. With non-use, the question is more complex, because the test results need to be correlated with its initial task, and questions answered: what exactly is meant by drug use, what are its specific patterns? because they can be quite different.

b) Criterion validity: can the test results be controlled by some external independent criteria? For example, high risks of drug use obtained from testing can be confirmed by the presence of actual drug use experience in respondents, which can be identified through questions separate from the test.

c) Construct validity: how logically do the test results relate to other phenomena? For example, how do the high risks of non-use obtained from testing relate to other personality traits and behavioral characteristics of an individual?

Recently, with the expansion of the test creation industry, so-called "test banks" (Test Banks vs Question Pools) have gained particular importance. Validated statements or scales (combined groups of statements) are entered into such banks and can subsequently be used by other users to compile various tests. The value of such banks increases if, for each item, the results of its empirical approbation and other data concerning its use in various tests, on which target groups, etc., are also provided. In such services, one can construct their own test by selecting its questions and scales using convenient search and insertion into the constructor. Thus, other users who wish to develop their own tests can save time and effort.

4 Reliability

A measurement instrument is considered reliable if it consistently yields the same results when used multiple times to measure the same object (under the same conditions), regardless of who applies it.

Reliability indicates that the results of the conducted study are close to the truth, while validity shows that the results truly pertain to the phenomenon being studied by the researcher. A valid study is automatically reliable, but the inverse is not necessarily true. A reliable study may not be valid.5 Standardization

The ultimate goal of standardization is always to obtain norms that allow converting "raw" data obtained during testing into standard scores, to then correctly interpret the final test indicators for specific individuals. Simply put, norms are a quantitative indicator (or several) based on which we assign a test subject to one category or another after testing, for example, answering questions like: is their risk of drug use high or low? do they belong to a risk group or not?

Without delving into complex standardization procedures, it is important to note here that standardization is an ongoing process that ensures the relevance of a diagnostic method and maintains user demand for it. Standardization is the process of developing a method in three directions.

a) Expansion of norms. For most tests, initial standardization is typically conducted on a limited contingent, resulting in an insufficient volume or representativeness of the sample. This is particularly characteristic of domestic psychodiagnostics, as developers often lack the practical ability to immediately provide a sufficiently large and representative sample for standardization. Therefore, over time, norms can be refined on more representative samples.

b) Specialization of norms. Creation of differentiated norms for different groups and for different practical purposes. For example, many tests are useful to norm separately for different age, gender, and professional groups. Differentiated standardization increases the user potential of the method and is considered one of the important indicators of test quality.

c) Updating norms. This work should be carried out constantly, at least approximately every 5 years, as norms lose their relevance over time. Over the past decades, general population changes have been observed that affect the behavior of large groups of people: the level of cognitive function development in children and even adults is growing, the level of depression and anxiety disorders is increasing, social norms related to behavior and health are changing, leading to a shift in respondents' evaluations, etc. See how long ago the norms for the diagnostic methods you use were adjusted!

6 Methodology Review

Psychometrics, like diagnostics in medicine, essentially functions as an economic sector where clients (test users and test-takers) have the right to receive a quality product (tests) for their money. Quality primarily refers to the safety and scientific validity of the results. Therefore, the history of centralized expertise for tests and other measurement instruments began in the USA as early as 1895, when the first Psychometrics Committee of the American Psychological Association was established. In 1938, the first edition of the still-existing "The Mental Measurements Yearbook (MMY) and Tests in Print (TIP)" was published. Its author, Oscar Buros, organized the review process by analogy with peer review of articles in scientific journals. Subsequently, a two-stage accreditation was developed. In the first stage, an expert visits the test developer/publisher, evaluating the organizational structure, test creation, its administration, psychometric methods, and safety procedures. Once this stage (test provider accreditation) is completed, the product accreditation stage begins. Two independent experts write their reviews. Today, the Buros Institute of Mental Measurements/Center for Testing is an independent agency at the University of Nebraska (Lincoln). Its database contains data from 900 experts. Currently, the Buros Center for Testing asks its experts to use APA, AERA & NCME standards during audits, as well as (when evaluating computerized tests) the Guidelines for Computer-Based Testing: the Association of Test Publishers (ATP, 2001).

7 Training and Supervision by Specialists

Test methods are intended for use by a wide range of specialists, often far removed from psychology and understanding the essence, capabilities, and limitations of psychological tests. Therefore, it is important that specialists in the development of such methods train those who will apply them, consult them, and supervise their work. Recently, the situation has significantly changed in many countries: to obtain the right to use any methods belonging to a certain complexity group, it is necessary to undergo training in universal competencies and receive a certificate verifying the user's qualification level against the requirements of the standard adopted in that country. Therefore, after the publication of a method, the following relevant tasks arise: a) training users and issuing them rights (certificates of right) to use a specific method; b) consulting on test administration and interpretation for users already applying the method; c) retraining users when new forms and modifications of the method are introduced. Modification refers to any changes made to the method by the authors themselves.

Modifications to the method include:

Method adaptation – this is the process of adjusting a method for use in new or changed conditions, or in relation to a new target group. The creation of an electronic version of the method can also be considered adaptation. As a rule, adaptation entails minor changes. Translation of a method into a new language or deep adaptation to the peculiarities of another culture – usually requires a profound revision of the method, so complex that in some cases it is deemed impractical compared to creating an entirely new method from scratch. ***

In conclusion, it must be emphasized that the creation of reliable psychodiagnostic methods is an extremely complex and expensive procedure, requiring an appropriate legal framework and a developed market for psychodiagnostic services, which are not available in all countries. Even the most famous names in global psychodiagnostics have created only one, sometimes slightly more, methods in their lifetime. Such work can be compared to creating masterpieces in art. Therefore, in many countries, the development of psychodiagnostic methods has long ceased to be the domain of individuals. Today, this is handled by collaborations involving numerous research centers, publishers, developers, data processing specialists, and other experts based on the principle of division of functions. Therefore, many tests do not have individual authors, but only an indication of the university or developing company.
